units.t: Optimization II — Five Ways Down One Valley

secs: s1
Why are we even talking about lines?
almost everything looks straight when you zoom in, so linear equations are the tool machine learning reaches for first.
s2
What is a vector, really?
a vector is an ordered list of numbers that you can add slot by slot and scale, and almost any data can be written that way.
s3
A small problem you can solve by hand
a system of linear equations is a set of rules that must all be true at once, and you solve it by subtracting rules to remove unknowns one at a time.
s4
The three fates: zero, one, or infinity
each equation is a straight line (or flat plane), and they can meet nowhere, at one point, or along a whole line, so a system has zero, one or infinitely many solutions.
s5
Meet the matrix — a spreadsheet with superpowers
a matrix is a grid of numbers, and multiplying two matrices means "row times column" for every cell, which is the same as doing one filter after another.
s6
One equation, three windows
Ax = b can be read as rules to obey (rows), ingredients to mix (columns), or a machine to run backwards, and switching windows is the key skill of linear algebra.
s7
A matrix is a Photoshop filter for space
a matrix moves space by sending î and ĵ to its columns, and its determinant is how much it scales area (or volume), with det = 0 meaning space got squashed flat.
s8
The undo button — the inverse
the inverse is the undo button for a matrix; it exists only when det A is not zero, and in real work we solve with elimination instead of computing it.
s9
A system with training wheels
when a system has infinitely many solutions, they all look like one particular answer plus any mix of the directions the matrix sends to zero.
The null space — the machine's blind spot
the null space holds every input the matrix sends to zero, and adding any of them to a solution gives another solution, which is why answers come in families.
Gaussian elimination — the algorithm
Gaussian elimination uses swap, scale and add-a-multiple to turn the augmented matrix into a staircase, without ever changing the solutions, and the staircase then shows the answer and the s
RREF — finish the job, and two tricks fall out
RREF keeps eliminating until every pivot is a lone 1, so solutions, null-space directions and even the inverse can be read straight off the page.
Rank — one number that settles everything
rank is the number of pivots, the number of truly independent rows and of columns, and comparing rank(A), rank([A|b]) and n tells you whether a system has zero, one or infinitely many soluti
The whole story, in five lines
a matrix moves space, elimination reveals what it did, and rank tells you whether Ax = b has zero, one or infinitely many answers.

s1
The universe upgrade
every object in machine learning is a list of numbers, and this unit maps the world those lists live in and the rules for moving around it.
s2
Groups — the bare skeleton of "combining things"
a group is any world where combining keeps you inside and every move can be undone.
s3
Vector spaces = group + scaling
a vector space is any world where you can add and scale freely and never fall off the board.
s4
Subspaces — spaces inside spaces
a subspace is a flat world through the origin where adding and scaling never take you outside.
s5
The promised passport: the null space is a subspace
whatever a matrix cannot see forms a subspace, because zero plus zero is zero and a stretched zero is still zero.
s6
Span — everywhere you can reach
the span is everywhere your arrows can take you, and it only grows when a new arrow points somewhere new.
s7
Linear independence — the art of non-redundancy
vectors are independent when the only walk that brings you home is the one where you never leave.
s8
The detector: elimination hunts redundancy
eliminate the columns, and every column without a pivot is exposed as a mix of the pivot columns before it.
s9
The recipes theorem — independence survives translation
with independent ingredients, dishes are independent exactly when their recipe cards are, so you can always check the cards instead.
Basis — the just-right toolkit
a basis is a set of directions that reaches everything with nothing to spare, so every vector gets exactly one address.
Dimension — how big is the board, really?
dimension is the number of independent directions a space really has, and every basis agrees on it.
Finding a basis — the algorithm
to shrink a pile of vectors to a basis, keep each vector only if it points outside the span of the ones you already kept.
The whole story, in six lines
know your space, spot the redundancy, find the span, and pick the smartest basis.

Practice arena — solved problems
s1
The quest for "similar"
machine learning keeps asking "how similar are these two things?", and this unit is about the rulers that answer it.
s2
Norms — what "length" is allowed to mean
a norm is any rule for length that scales properly, allows no shortcuts, and gives zero only to "nowhere".
s2d
The dot product — one number that reads two vectors
multiply matching entries and add them up; the total says how much two lists agree, and a list's agreement with itself is its length squared.
s3
Inner products — the blueprint under the dot product
an inner product is any agreement score that is fair with sums, the same both ways, and always positive for a list with itself.
s4
The engine room — symmetric positive-definite matrices
to design a ruler, pick a symmetric matrix that gives every non-zero arrow a positive length squared, and test it with the top-left number and the determinant.
s5
Lengths, distances — and the inequality that runs everything
length and distance come free with every inner product, and the score can never beat the product of the lengths, just as a shadow can never beat the stick.
s6
Angles — the similarity dial
cosine similarity is the agreement score with the lengths divided out, so it measures direction only: +1 same, 0 unrelated, −1 opposite.
s7
The high-dimension miracle
in many dimensions, random arrows are almost always at right angles, so real similarity stands out clearly.
s8
Orthogonality is in the eye of the ruler
change the ruler and the same two arrows can stop being at a right angle.
s9
Orthonormal matrices — the motions that don't lie
a matrix with AᵀA=I turns or flips space like a stiff tile, so every length and angle survives.
The shadow machine — projection
to find a shadow, ask for the leftover to be at a right angle, and the amount comes out as ⟨a,b⟩/⟨b,b⟩.
Gram–Schmidt — cleaning a messy basis
Gram–Schmidt turns any crooked basis into a square one by cutting off shadows and resizing to length 1.
The whole story, in five lines

Practice arena — solved problems
s1
What survives the machine?
a matrix moves everything, but it has simple fingerprints: one number for how much it grows space, and special directions it only stretches.
s2
The determinant — how much a matrix grows area
the determinant is the signed area of the tile the unit square becomes: its size is the growth, a minus means flipped, and zero means squashed flat for good.
s3
Computing it — small pieces and the lazy row
break a big determinant into small signed pieces along the laziest line, or eliminate to a triangle and multiply the diagonal.
s4
The trace — a quick pulse check
the trace adds up the diagonal, ignores the order of a product, and turns out to be the sum of the eigenvalues.
s5
Eigenvectors — the directions a matrix cannot turn
an eigenvector is a direction the matrix only stretches, and its eigenvalue says by how much: Ax=λx.
s6
Hunting eigenvalues — the characteristic equation
eigenvalues are the values of λ where (A-λ I)=0; they always add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
s7
The Spectral Theorem — symmetric matrices come apart cleanly
every symmetric matrix has a hidden right-angle grain, so it is just turn, stretch along the grain, turn back: A=QΛ Q^ᵀ.
s8
The theorem in 3D — a ball becomes an egg
in 3D a symmetric matrix squeezes the ball into an egg along three right-angle axes, and the volume grows by the product of the three eigenvalues.
s9
When nothing lines up — turns and complex eigenvalues
a matrix that turns has no real eigen-directions, and its complex eigenvalues θ± iθ are the turn written as a number.
Cholesky — the square root of a matrix
a positive-definite matrix has a triangular square root L, found corner by corner, and L is exactly the lens that turns plain random numbers into realistic data.
The fine print — missing directions, and the bridge to ML
only non-symmetric matrices with repeated eigenvalues can run short of eigen-directions, and the data matrix A^ᵀA never does.
The whole story, in five lines

Practice arena — solved problems
s1
Taking things apart — the oldest trick in mathematics
a decomposition rewrites a matrix as a few simple moves — turn, resize, turn — without changing what it does.
s2
The goal — diagonal matrices are easy
a diagonal matrix is easy because each axis minds its own business — so this unit is a hunt for the diagonal hiding inside every matrix.
s3
Diagonalizable — same machine, better glasses
A=PDP⁻¹ just says: put A's eigenvectors in the columns of P and their eigenvalues in D.
s4
Step 1 · Spectral — the perfect case, read a new way
a symmetric matrix is a set of perpendicular directions, each turned up by its own eigenvalue — nothing more.
s5
Step 2 · Eigendecomposition — the matrix's own language
P⁻¹ translates into the matrix's own language, D does a simple resize there, and P translates back.
s6
Where eigendecomposition fails — and the fix
eigendecomposition fails whenever one set of axes must serve both input and output — the shear, the rotation, and every rectangular matrix.
s7
Step 3 · SVD — two frames, every matrix, no exceptions
every matrix is turn · resize · turn — V^ᵀ, then Σ, then U — no exceptions.
s8
Building U, Σ, V — the symmetric-matrix bridge
to break down A, break down the symmetric round trip A^ᵀA instead: V and the σ's fall out, and u_i=Av_i/σ_i finishes the job.
s9
Seeing a rectangular matrix — 2-D in, 3-D out
a rectangular matrix maps one world into another: its image is a flat slice of the bigger world, and u_3 is the direction it can never reach.
The layer cake — low-rank approximation, live
sort the layers biggest first and keep the top few — the best possible summary of any matrix, whether it is a photograph or a table of tastes.
The spectral norm — and the family portrait
σ_1 is the loudest a matrix can ever be, and σ_1/σ_2 says how uneven its boosts are.
The whole story, in five lines
find the two frames and the sorted stretches, and any matrix becomes simple enough to read, repeat, undo and compress.

s1
You are standing in fog, and you want to get down
training is walking downhill in fog: you cannot see the valley, but you can always feel the slope under your feet, and that is enough.
s2
The derivative, built from a shrinking triangle
the derivative is the slope of a two-point line as the two points squeeze into one, and it exists exactly where the curve looks straight up close.
s3
Four rules, and the only one that really matters
rates in a row multiply, and a deep network is a long row, which is why the chain rule runs machine learning.
s4
Taylor — rebuilding a whole function out of its derivatives
a Taylor polynomial copies a function's value, slope, bend and more at one point, and the k! keeps the copies from disturbing each other.
s5
Many knobs at once — partial derivatives
to take a partial derivative, freeze every other input and differentiate as usual.
s6
The gradient — a compass that always points uphill
the gradient puts all the partial derivatives in one arrow: it points steepest uphill, its length is the steepness, and minus it is the direction of training.
s7
The five shapes a derivative can take
count before you compute: one sensitivity per (output, input) pair, with outputs as rows and inputs as columns.
s8
The Jacobian — a local rulebook for a curved map
the Jacobian is the matrix a curved map turns into when you zoom in close.
s9
The Jacobian determinant — area, invertibility, one warning
J is the local area factor: non-zero means you can undo the map nearby, but not always everywhere at once.
The chain rule becomes matrix multiplication — and that is backpropagation
backpropagation is the chain rule as matrix multiplication, done from the loss end backwards so that nothing bigger than a row is ever built.
Walking down the valley
gradient descent is w w-η∇ L: the gradient picks the direction, and η decides how far to trust it.
Fine print worth knowing
rows versus columns is a habit, the order of matrix factors is a rule, a corner has no derivative, and the giant four-way table is used but never stored.
What to carry forward
nudge, measure, divide, shrink: that one move, kept tidy with shapes, is all of differentiation for machine learning.

Practice arena — solved problems
s1
The million-knob problem
training needs the loss's slope for every knob at every step, and finding them one knob at a time would cost one run of the network per knob.
s2
Baby steps — the computation graph
write the function as a chain of easy steps; values flow forward, and blame v=∂ f/∂ v flows backward from f=1 to every step.
s3
The whole algorithm is two rules
backpropagation is two rules — multiply the small slopes along each path, add the paths — done so that no path is walked twice.
sproof
Why you can trust the two rules — the chain rule, proved
a derivative is a "straight line plus fading leftover" promise; chaining promises multiplies slopes, side-by-side routes add, and row-times-column is both rules at once.
s4
The recipe, written once and for all
set f=1, then let every value send each parent its own blame times a small slope — one right-to-left sweep prices every knob.
s5
One neuron, trained by your own hands
compute the blame δ=∂ L/∂ z once, and every knob feeding z reads its slope off it — then step downhill and the loss really falls.
s6
A whole layer at once — backprop with matrices
scale the blame by each neuron's slope, then weights get δ^(Z) x^ᵀ, biases get δ^(Z), and the layer below gets A^ᵀδ^(Z) — four lines, the inner loop of deep learning.
s7
The gradient cookbook — five rules you'll use forever
five recipes — dot product, outer product, the B+B^ᵀ doubling and least squares — give almost every small slope a real model needs.
s8
Why it's so cheap — one sweep, everything reused
all the layer slopes share one long start — carry it once, from the loss end, and the whole set costs a single sweep.
s9
Linearization — the slope as a stand-in for the function
f( x_0)+∇ f( x_0)^ᵀ( x- x_0) is the best straight-line stand-in near x_0 — the promise every gradient-descent step relies on.
Fine print worth knowing
autodiff is exact like the paper method and cheap like one run of the program, which is why nudging survives only as a checker.
What to carry forward
loss.backward() is this unit run by a for-loop — one backward sweep through the graph hands every knob its slope.
spractice
Practice arena — solved problems
s1
Every smooth curve is secretly a polynomial — up close
a Taylor polynomial copies a curve's height, slope and bend at one spot, and this unit proves why that copy works and how far it can be trusted.
s2
The flat spot — Rolle's theorem
a smooth trail with the same height at both ends must be level somewhere in between, and a sharp corner cancels the promise.
s3
Average equals instantaneous — the mean value theorem
somewhere on the way your instant speed equals your average speed, and written as a formula this is already a straight-line copy with no error.
s4
The Rolle ladder — one flat spot per rung
a function that is very flat at a and zero at b passes one zero down per derivative, until its n-th derivative is zero somewhere in between.
s5
Taylor's theorem, built by hand
make the gap flat at a and zero at b, run the Rolle ladder, and the leftover turns out to be the next term measured at a secret point.
s6
How big is the error? — the remainder in your hands
you never learn c, but a worst-case size M for the next derivative turns the leftover into a firm promise, |R_n|≤ M|x-a|^n/n!.
s7
MacLaurin's series — and why the factorial always wins
a MacLaurin series is Taylor at 0, and the series for e^x, x and x always settle down because n! eventually grows faster than any |x|^n.
s8
Two variables — walk along a line and it is one variable again
along a straight walk the landscape is a one-variable curve, and its bend h²f_xx+2hkf_xy+k²f_yy is where the Hessian comes from.
s9
At a flat point, the second-order term decides
at a level spot the slope part is zero, so the bend Q alone decides whether you are in a valley, on a peak, or at a pass.
smat
Taylor in matrix form — and how to remember it
the Hessian packs the bends into a table, and the step sandwiches it, so many-variable Taylor reads exactly like the one-variable formula.
The judge of extrema — the Hessian
the Hessian's discriminant, its corner determinants and its eigenvalues are three ways to read one verdict — bowl, upside-down bowl, or saddle.
The judge at work — six landscapes
find every level spot, judge each one with its own Hessian, and when D=0 admit that the bends cannot decide.
Why a learning machine cares — curvature, conditioning, and the saddle problem
near its bottom a loss is its own quadratic clone, so the Hessian decides how hard training is, and its inverse gives Newton's one-jump step.
What to carry forward
Taylor copies a function near a point with a guaranteed error, and the Hessian in that copy judges every valley a learning machine finds.

Practice arena — solved problems
s1
Downhill in the fog
learning is a walk in fog — feel the slope, step the other way, repeat — which works in any number of dimensions, but finds only the valley below where you started.
s2
Why there is a landscape at all
say what "wrong" means, and a landscape appears by itself — one height for every setting of the knobs — with a slope that says which way the line should move.
s3
Where the walk ends — flat ground comes in three kinds
the walk stops on level ground; the bend tells a valley from a hilltop or a saddle; and you land in the valley below where you started.
s4
The rule, and the trench that makes it zig-zag
on a bowl the slope is a spring, ∇ f=A x+ b; a trench has a stiff spring and a soft one, so one stride bounces across it while it crawls along it.
s5
How long a step — the bouncing ball
each step multiplies the distance to the bottom by 1-γλ, so keep γ<2/λ_ — and the gap between the stiffest and softest directions is what makes the walk zig-zag.
s6
Let the ground choose the stride — line search
slide along the downhill line until the ground stops dropping — there the new slope is at a right angle to your step — and on a bowl the best stride is g^ᵀ g/ g^ᵀA g.
s7
Finding the bottom of one line — higher or lower?
when there is no formula for the best stride, trap it in a bracket and squeeze — or, like real training, take Armijo's "good enough" stride.
s8
Bold early, careful late — schedules and the bold driver
the learning rate is a speed that should drop as you near the bottom — on a timer (exponential, inverse, step) or by feel (the bold driver).
s9
Is my compass even right? — the known weight
check a coded slope by nudging a few knobs; the two-way nudge is far more accurate, until the nudge is so tiny that rounding takes over.
svar
Three ways to walk — batch, minibatch, stochastic
batch, minibatch and stochastic differ only in how much data they read per step; a random spoonful is right on average, so per data read the noisy walkers win — which is why deep learning us
Noise, tamed — and noise as a friend
a noisy slope is a shaking hand — a fixed stride leaves a jitter cloud, a shrinking stride closes it, and the same shake can hop a walker out of a shallow dip.
What to carry forward
gradient descent is one reflex — step against the slope — and this whole unit is about how big, how exact and how cheap that step should be.

Practice arena — solved problems
s1
The bill for being wrong — and why the squares are squares
the bill is the total area of one square patch per data row, and its slope is each row's miss times that row, added up — the same recipe for one knob or a billion.
s2
The parachute drop — where you start
start small and random — and when the numbers explode anyway, blame the feature's size squared in the factor 1-2η x², not the place you started.
s3
Full marks by memorising — knobs versus facts
with more knobs than facts a zero bill is free and so means nothing — the memoriser hits every training row and still cannot see the one feature that matters.
s4
The hair-trigger and the stiff knob
a knob's sensitivity is its feature's size squared, so features of different sizes turn one stride into a fire hose on one knob and a drip on the other — and only rescaling the features can
s5
Three ways to fix the units — centre, standardise, min–max
centring slides, standardising squeezes, min–max boxes — all three put every column on the same scale, and all three treat new data with the training numbers.
s6
The wrong valley — the watershed and the combination lock
the side of the watershed you start on decides the valley you reach, and with many knobs the valleys multiply like the settings of a combination lock — so restarts alone cannot save you.
s7
The salt flat — where the walk slows to nothing
each step is stride times tilt, so a plateau — small tilt, but no valley — can swallow hundreds of thousands of steps.
s8
The canyon — why the fastest way down is the wrong way down
in a canyon each direction shrinks by its own factor 1-ηλ, the steepest wall sets the speed limit, and , steepest over gentlest, tells you how much of the walk is wasted bouncing.
s9
Why the compass crosses the contour lines at a right angle
a step along a contour changes nothing, so the gradient crosses every contour at a right angle — which points at the bottom only when the contours are circles.
Change the units, not the model — the canyon becomes a bowl
the bill feels each column squared, so dividing every column by its own spread levels every wall — the canyon becomes a bowl, the safe stride grows a hundredfold, and the model and the data'
The training clinic — read the loss curve like a doctor
every failure in this unit leaves its own shape on the loss curve, and every fix either reshapes the landscape or gives the walker better instincts.
What to carry forward
most training troubles are a badly shaped landscape, and the cheapest way to reshape it is to put every feature on the same scale.

Practice arena — solved problems
s1
Your feet feel the tilt, not the turn
The slope tells you which way is down but not how long it lasts, so one shared stride must suit every direction at once — and when directions differ tenfold, no stride can.
s2
Momentum — give the walker weight
Momentum adds a faded copy of the last move, so pushes that agree pile up to 1/(1-β) times a plain step and pushes that flip cancel — at the cost of overshoot, where the loss may rise for a
s3
AdaGrad — a stride for each knob, from a record that never clears
Divide each knob's step by the root of everything it has ever felt, and the first step is exactly α for every knob — but the record never clears, so the brake never lifts.
s4
RMSProp — judge by recent form
Swap the permanent record for a fading one and the stride survives all the way down — at the price of a first step that is 1/√1-ρ times too big, because an average that starts at zero is a w
s5
Adam — two notebooks and a warm-up
Adam keeps a signed average and a squared average for every knob, steps by their ratio so disagreement cancels and loudness divides out, and uses a warm-up rate α_t that makes the first step
s6
Five walkers, one valley — and the dial that decides the race
Plain descent's safe stride is set by the steepest direction and its speed by the gentlest, so it pays the condition number in steps — while every adaptive method divides each slope by its o
s7
Then someone builds a wall
Put a wall in a problem and the answer moves onto the wall, where the slope is not zero — so "stop where it is flat" must be replaced, starting by writing every problem as f with e=0 and g_i
s8
Pushing a box against a wall
You stop when nothing is left to slide along the fence, so ∇ f and ∇ g lie on one line with a stretch µ≥0 between them — and that stretch is about to become a price.
s9
Turn the wall into a fine
You cannot differentiate an infinite wall but you can differentiate a straight line, and letting the guard raise the line's slope rebuilds the wall exactly — so L=f+λ e+Σµ_i g_i with µ_i≥0 i
Room left, and the rule that falls out of it
Write the room left as a square, differentiate, and out comes µ_ig_i=0 — either there is room and the fine is zero, or you are touching and the fine may be positive.
Five conditions, and checking every case
KKT is "set every derivative to zero" on the Lagrangian plus the sign rule, and room-or-fine turns it into 2^m cases to check, most of which die on a negative fine.
Which problems you can trust
A bowl never rises above its strings and never dips below its tangents — and on a bowl with bowl fences, a point that passes the five conditions is the answer; anywhere else it is only a can
Who moves first — and what a wall is worth
Letting the guard move first gives the dual, which is the lowest of many straight lines — so it is always a hill and always a lower bound — and the fine it hands back is the price of the wal
Two points and a line — where all of this is going
The widest road is the smallest 12w² that clears every point, its dual has one fine per training point, and room-or-fine makes almost all of them zero — so the machine rests on a few support
What to carry forward
Optimisers divide each step by what that knob has felt, and fenced problems turn every wall into a price — and the price tells you which walls matter.
